query: For high-entropy alloys intended as intermediate materials in plasma-facing reactor components, what single intervention could improve heat-transfer capability while preserving structural integrity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the expected outcome compared with current intermediate-layer performance, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partial substitution of Ta with Ti in the high‐entropy alloy intermediate layer will improve the heat-transfer capability while maintaining structural integrity under plasma‐facing reactor conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐entropy alloy intermediate layer formulated with full Ta content as currently used.
generation.intervention: Substitute part of the Ta with Ti via mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering.
generation.conditions: Operational temperatures up to approximately 700°C under mechanical load conditions typical of plasma-facing reactor environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The retained multiphase microstructure with modified lattice dynamics due to the lower average atomic mass from Ti substitution.
generation.mechanism: Ti substitution is expected to decrease the alloy’s average atomic mass leading to reduced phonon scattering and improved thermal conduction, while its chemical compatibility helps preserve the existing microstructural integrity and mechanical strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy should display a measurable increase in thermal conductivity relative to the baseline (full Ta) alloy while exhibiting no significant degradation in mechanical properties or microstructural stability under operational conditions.
generation.baseline: The current high‐entropy alloy intermediate layer with no Ti substitution, characterized by its standard thermal and mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected for optimized substitution levels (likely up to 20–30% replacement of Ta by Ti); higher levels may risk destabilizing the microstructure and degrading mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of heat-transfer improvement and the optimal substitution level require further targeted computational and experimental investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of high-entropy alloy samples with graduated levels of Ta-to-Ti substitution (e.g., 0%, 10%, 20%, and 30%). Process them via mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering. Under controlled laboratory conditions, subject the samples to thermal cycling and mechanical loading that mimic plasma-facing reactor conditions (up to 700°C).
measurements: Microstructural stability (using electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with Ti substitution do not show a statistically significant increase in thermal conductivity compared to the baseline sample, or if their mechanical properties and microstructural phases deteriorate significantly under the test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.
